This FOMC statement is hawkish: policy rates were lifted to 3–3.25% with guidance for “ongoing increases,” and quantitative tightening continues. In the literature, such a response aligns with Taylor-rule principles that call for raising the policy rate more than one-for-one when inflation exceeds target, helping re-anchor expectations and preserve credibility (Goodfriend; Taylor; Walsh). The emphasis on returning inflation to 2% echoes lessons from the Volcker disinflation—that decisive tightening reduces long-run costs of inflation even if near-term activity slows. Balance sheet runoff is consistent with research showing central banks influence the yield curve and term premia via asset holdings (Cochrane; Piazzesi), tightening financial conditions beyond the policy rate alone. The statement’s recognition of the Ukraine war as a supply shock is notable; theory cautions against fully accommodating such shocks, instead focusing on expectations and gradual real-side adjustment (Walsh; Goodfriend). At the same time, robust employment buffers downside risks, and DSGE and empirical work (e.g., Lubik and Schorfheide; Orphanides) underscore the importance of data monitoring and avoiding mismeasurement-driven policy errors. Netting these, the tone is negative for near-term growth but supportive of medium-term inflation control and credibility.
